title: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
summary: Why models that read raw UTF-8 bytes avoid tokenizer blind spots, why that is costly, and how MegaByte, SpaceByte and the Byte Latent Transformer group bytes into patches to make it scale.
outcomes: Explain why byte-level models cost more per byte and why feed-forward layers, not attention, dominate that cost
Compute forward FLOPs per byte for a patched model from global and local parameter counts
Apply entropy patching with global and monotonic thresholds to a byte sequence
Describe BLT's local encoder, hash n-gram embeddings, latent Transformer and local decoder
Weigh byte models against BPE on compute, robustness and character-level tasks

lessons.title: Why drop the tokenizer, and why raw bytes are expensive

blocks.md: A GPT, as you built it, never sees text. A **tokenizer** first maps the text to ids from a fixed vocabulary learned by BPE, and the model only ever sees those ids. The BLT paper (Pagnoni et al., 2024) lists what this costs: models are sensitive to domain shifts and to noisy input, they lack *orthographic* knowledge (how words are spelled), and they are inequitable across languages because the vocabulary was fitted mostly to some languages.

The token id for `strawberry` carries no explicit trace of its letters. To count the r's, the model must have memorized the spelling of that id. A **tokenizer-free** model removes the fixed vocabulary and reads the raw **bytes** of the text instead, so every letter is in its input.

Text on disk is almost always **UTF-8**, which encodes each Unicode character (code point) as 1 to 4 bytes (RFC 3629). ASCII characters take 1 byte. Every other character starts with a *lead byte* followed by *continuation bytes* of the form `10xxxxxx`. A byte model therefore needs only 256 input ids, can represent any string in any language, and never sees an unknown token.

blocks.title: The same words as UTF-8 bytes (hex)

scenes.caption: English letters are ASCII, 1 byte each: hello is 5 characters and 5 bytes. A byte model with 256 input ids reads this directly.
In café, the accented e is one character but 2 bytes (c3 a9): a lead byte plus one continuation byte. 4 characters become 5 bytes.
Cyrillic takes 2 bytes per character and Japanese 3, so 6 Russian characters are 12 bytes and 3 Japanese characters are 9. Colors alternate per character.
Devanagari code points take 3 bytes each: this Hindi word is 6 code points and 18 bytes. Byte sequences are longest exactly where subword vocabularies are usually weakest.

blocks.prompt: A Transformer spends roughly the same compute on every position it processes. Llama 3's tokenizer averages about 4.4 bytes per token on BLT's training mix. If you feed the same text as raw bytes to a model with the same parameters, roughly how much more compute does it spend?
blocks.reveal: About **4.4 times** more, because there are about 4.4 times more positions. The extra cost is not mainly attention: a forward pass with $m$ non-embedding parameters over $T$ positions costs roughly $2mT$ FLOPs (the approximation MegaByte uses), and that term is linear in $T$. Making each position cheaper or making fewer positions is the only way out.

blocks.caption: m = non-embedding parameters, T = number of positions. Per-position feed-forward and projection layers dominate: MegaByte notes self-attention is only 1.4% of GPT-3's FLOPs.

blocks.md: Common misconception: byte models are slow because attention is quadratic. Efficient attention helps small models, but the BLT authors point out that at scale the cost is dominated by the large feed-forward layers that run on **every** position. Fewer positions through the big network is what matters.

**ByT5** (Xue et al., 2022) showed the simplest approach works: take T5, feed UTF-8 bytes with 256 byte ids plus 3 special ids (padding, end of sequence, an unused UNK), and keep everything else standard. Two changes helped: the parameters freed from the vocabulary matrices went into the layers, and the encoder was made 3 times deeper than the decoder. Its pre-training masks spans of about 20 bytes instead of about 3 tokens.

blocks.title: Share of parameters in the vocabulary matrices

scenes.caption: mT5 (multilingual subword vocabulary): the vocabulary and softmax matrices take 85% of the Small model and 66% of the 582M-parameter Base model.
ByT5 at the same total size: the 256-byte vocabulary is at most 0.3% of parameters at every size, so almost all capacity sits in the Transformer layers.

blocks.md: The price was speed. ByT5 reports inference 3.7 to 6.4 times slower than mT5 on document summarization and 6.4 to 9.5 times slower on XNLI classification, where inputs are long and outputs are short. Every byte goes through every layer. The rest of this course is about avoiding that.

Bytes remove the vocabulary and its blind spots, but multiply the number of positions by roughly 4. Since compute is about $2mT$, a byte model is only practical if the big network runs on far fewer positions than there are bytes.

blocks.question: A team swaps a 128K BPE vocabulary for raw bytes and keeps the same 7B Transformer, using FlashAttention for speed. Training throughput in bytes per second drops about 4x. What is the main reason?
options: FlashAttention does not support a vocabulary of 256
Attention is quadratic, so 4x longer sequences cost 16x more
There are about 4x more positions and the feed-forward and projection layers run once per position
The 256-way softmax is more expensive than a 128K-way softmax
blocks.explain: Compute scales roughly as 2mT, linear in the number of positions T. With about 4 bytes per token there are about 4x more positions, so throughput per byte drops about 4x. Attention is a small share at this scale, and a 256-way softmax is far cheaper than a 128K-way one.

blocks.question: Why can a byte-level model never hit an out-of-vocabulary input?
options: Its vocabulary is the 256 possible byte values, and any UTF-8 text is a sequence of bytes
It learns new tokens during inference
It maps rare characters to an UNK id
UTF-8 has only 256 characters
blocks.explain: Every string, in any script, is a sequence of bytes 0 to 255, so the input vocabulary is complete by construction. UTF-8 covers all of Unicode by using 1 to 4 bytes per character, not by having 256 characters.

lessons.title: Patches: run the big model once per group of bytes

blocks.md: **MegaByte** (Yu et al., 2023) groups bytes into **patches** of a fixed size $P$. A large **global** Transformer runs once per patch, over $T/P$ positions, and a small **local** Transformer predicts the $P$ bytes inside each patch, one byte at a time, conditioned on the global output. Most bytes are easy (finishing a word after its first letters), so the expensive network is not needed for every byte.

blocks.caption: From MegaByte's analysis: m_g = global parameters, m_l = local parameters, T = bytes. When m_g is much larger than m_l, the cost falls almost as 1/P.

blocks.md: Attention gets cheaper too. The global model attends over $T/P$ positions, costing $O(T^2/P^2)$, and the local model runs $T/P$ sequences of length $P$, costing $O(TP)$. Choosing $P = T^{1/3}$ gives $O(T^{4/3})$ overall. But as lesson 1 showed, the feed-forward savings matter more.

blocks.title: Forward FLOPs per byte versus patch size

scenes.caption: Simplified model (ignores attention and cross-attention). Defaults match BLT's 8B config: 6.4B global, 20M encoder plus 120M decoder local parameters. Without patching every byte costs 13.08 GFLOPs.
At P = 4.4 (Llama 3's bytes per token) the cost is 3.19 GFLOPs per byte; at P = 8 it is 1.88, 41% less. The local term 2L = 0.28 is a floor that patching cannot remove.

Grow the global model to 8B: now P = 4.4 costs 3.92 and P = 8 costs 2.28 (the marked points stay at 6.4B). 8B at P = 8 is still cheaper than 6.4B at P = 4.4: longer patches buy room for a bigger model.

blocks.md: Fixed-size patches have two problems, according to the BLT paper. Compute is not spent where it is needed: a whole global step may go to predicting whitespace in code, while dense text such as math gets too little. And patching is not contextual: the same word is split differently depending on where it lands.

blocks.title: Three ways to cut the same 22 bytes

scenes.caption: Strided patching (MegaByte) every 4 bytes gives 6 patches. The first the is one patch, but the second is cut into on_t and he_m: the same word looks different to the global model each time.
Space patching (SpaceByte) starts a patch after each space-like byte, so every word gets its own global step: 6 patches, and both copies of the are cut identically.
Preview: entropy patching with a toy model (lesson 3) gives 5 patches. It merges on_the_ into one patch because the whole phrase is predictable after on.

blocks.md: **SpaceByte** (Slagle, 2024) calls a byte *space-like* if it is not a Latin letter, a digit, or a UTF-8 continuation byte, and runs the larger blocks after space-like bytes. The hardest byte to predict is usually the first of a word, so this spends compute where it is needed. But it cannot vary the patch size, and it does not fit languages and domains without clear spaces.

Why not just use longer BPE tokens? A bigger vocabulary makes tokens longer, but it also grows the embedding table and the output softmax. The BLT paper notes Llama 3 raised the average token from 3.7 to 4.4 bytes at the cost of a 4x larger embedding table. A **patch** has no vocabulary at all: the encoder turns any byte group into a vector, so patch size is a free knob.
A patch is a group of bytes that the big model treats as one position, with no fixed vocabulary. Average patch size sets the compute: forward cost per byte is about $2(m_g/P + m_\ell)$.

blocks.question: Using the simplified cost $2(m_g/P + m_\ell)$ with $m_g$ = 6.4B and $m_\ell$ = 0.14B, what is the forward cost per byte at $P$ = 6?
options: About 13.1 GFLOPs
About 1.07 GFLOPs
About 2.41 GFLOPs
About 3.19 GFLOPs
blocks.explain: 2 x (6.4/6 + 0.14) = 2 x (1.067 + 0.14) = 2.41 GFLOPs. 13.1 is the unpatched cost, 3.19 is P = 4.4, and 1.07 forgets the factor 2 and the local term.

blocks.question: Which weakness is shared by strided and space patching but fixed by a patcher driven by prediction difficulty?
options: Both need a fixed vocabulary
Neither can split a word into more than one patch
Neither lets you tune the average patch size
Neither decides boundaries from how hard the upcoming bytes are to predict
blocks.explain: Strided patching cuts every P bytes, and space patching cuts at spaces; neither looks at how predictable the text is. Strided patching does let you tune P (so the third option is wrong for it), and neither uses a vocabulary.

lessons.title: Entropy patching: spend compute where the next byte is hard

blocks.md: BLT's answer is **entropy patching**: train a small byte-level language model $p_e$, and start a new patch wherever it is uncertain about the next byte. Uncertainty is measured by the **entropy** of its next-byte distribution. A peaked distribution (the next byte is obvious) has low entropy; a flat one has high entropy.

blocks.tex: H(x_i) = -\sum_{v \in \mathcal{V}} p_e(x_i = v \mid x_{<i}) \, \ln p_e(x_i = v \mid x_{<i})
blocks.caption: Next-byte entropy over the byte vocabulary V. The released BLT code computes it in nats (natural log). The maximum, for a uniform distribution over 256 bytes, is ln 256 = 5.55 nats.

blocks.md: To see it on real numbers, we use a toy entropy model: counts of the next byte given the previous 2 bytes, trained on a 147-byte corpus about cats, dogs and mats, with add-0.05 smoothing over the 15 distinct bytes in that corpus. BLT's actual entropy model is a 100M-parameter Transformer (14 layers, hidden size 512, 512-byte sliding window).

blocks.code:
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
import math
corpus = (b"the cat sat on the mat. the dog sat on the log. "
          b"a cat and a dog sat on a mat. the cat ate the rat. "
          b"the rat sat on the hat. on the mat the cat sat. ")
alphabet = sorted(set(corpus))          # 15 distinct bytes
counts = defaultdict(Counter)
for i in range(len(corpus)):
    counts[corpus[max(0, i - 2):i]][corpus[i]] += 1

def entropy(ctx, k=0.05):
    c = counts[ctx]; n = sum(c.values())
    ps = [(c[v] + k) / (n + k * len(alphabet)) for v in alphabet]
    return -sum(p * math.log(p) for p in ps)

print(round(entropy(b"e "), 2), round(entropy(b"ca"), 2))  # 2.01 0.81
blocks.caption: Toy 2-byte-context entropy model used for every number in this lesson.

scenes.caption: After the e and space of the, many words can follow. The mass is spread over c, m, r and more: entropy 2.01 nats. This is a hard prediction, worth a global step.
After ca, the corpus only ever continued with t, so t gets 0.853 and the rest is smoothing: entropy 0.81 nats. The local model can handle this byte cheaply.

blocks.md: Given entropies, BLT tests two boundary rules. The **global constraint** starts a patch at byte $t$ when $H(x_t)$ exceeds a threshold $\theta_g$. The **approximate monotonic constraint** starts one when entropy *jumps* by more than $\theta_r$ from the previous byte, so a patch is a stretch where entropy is roughly decreasing.

blocks.title: Entropy patching on the cat sat on the mat

scenes.caption: Toy-model entropy of each byte given the 2 bytes before it (the text follows a previous sentence ending in a period and space). Peaks sit at word starts: c and m at 2.01, s and o at 1.54.

Global threshold 1.6: only bytes above it start patches (red; the first byte, at 1.45, is red because it always starts one). 3 patches: the_, then cat_sat_on_the_ as one long patch, then mat. Average 7.3 bytes per patch.
Threshold 1.2: s and o now also qualify. 5 patches (the_, cat_, sat_, on_the_, mat), average 4.4 bytes. Note on_the_ stays together: after on_ the toy model is fairly sure what comes.
Threshold 0.9: spaces (1.05), a and t of mat (0.97) and t of the (1.09) also cross it. 10 patches, average 2.2 bytes: more global steps, more compute.
Monotonic rule with a jump threshold of 0.3 instead: a patch starts when entropy rises by more than 0.3 over the previous byte. 7 patches: the_, cat_, sat, _, on_, the_, mat.

blocks.prompt: In the threshold 1.2 scene, the second the is not its own patch, but the first the is. Why does the global model get no separate step for the second the?
blocks.reveal: Patch starts depend on context, not on the word. The first the begins the text, and position 0 always starts a patch. The second follows on_, and the toy model sees only the last 2 bytes, n_, which the corpus continues with t 4 times out of 5, so this t has entropy 1.09, below 1.2. The model judges it predictable and lets the local layers handle it inside the on_the_ patch.

blocks.md: The threshold is a dial on compute. BLT picks it to hit a target average patch size on the training mix, and keeps bytes per batch constant across settings so larger patches do not get an unfair advantage in context. For its 8B entropy-patched model the authors also changed the threshold at inference from 0.6 to 0.1, which improved task scores at the cost of more global steps.

Patching must also work during generation, when future bytes do not exist yet. BLT calls a scheme **incremental** if patching a prefix gives the same boundaries as patching the full text and then truncating. Entropy patching is incremental because $H(x_t)$ depends only on earlier bytes. BPE is not: the same prefix can be tokenized differently depending on what follows.

blocks.caption: Incremental patching property from the BLT paper.

blocks.md: Entropy depends on context, which can backfire. On a few-shot MMLU prompt, repeated phrases became very predictable, so they were swallowed into huge patches (the paper calls this entropy drift). The fix for the large run: reset the entropy model's context at newlines and use the monotonic rule.
Entropy patching spends a global step where the next byte is hard to predict and lets cheap local layers handle predictable runs. The threshold sets the average patch size, and therefore the compute.

blocks.question: You lower the global entropy threshold from 1.2 to 0.9 in the toy example. What happens?
options: Patch count drops from 5 to 3, saving compute
Patches get shorter (10 instead of 5), so the global model runs twice as often
Nothing changes, because boundaries come from spaces
The local decoder's vocabulary grows
blocks.explain: More bytes exceed a lower threshold, so more patches start: 10 patches of 2.2 bytes on average instead of 5 of 4.4. Each patch is one global step, so global compute roughly doubles. Raising the threshold (to 1.6) is what gives 3 patches.

blocks.question: Why can BPE tokenization not be used to decide patch boundaries while generating byte by byte?
options: BPE needs a GPU
BPE vocabularies are too small
BPE boundaries for a prefix can change once later bytes arrive, so it is not incremental
BPE only works on ASCII
blocks.explain: During generation BLT must decide whether the current byte starts a patch before future bytes exist. Entropy uses only past bytes, so its decisions never change. BPE merges depend on what follows, so the same prefix can be split differently.

lessons.title: Inside BLT: local encoder, latent Transformer, local decoder

blocks.md: BLT has three Transformer parts. A small **local encoder** turns bytes into patch vectors. A large **latent (global) Transformer** runs once per patch. A small **local decoder** turns patch outputs back into next-byte predictions. A separate entropy model only decides where patches start.

scenes.caption: Step 1: the entropy model reads the bytes and marks patch starts. This runs during data loading in training, separate from the main model.
Step 2: each byte gets an embedding plus hashed n-gram embeddings, then a light encoder layer. Cross-attention pools the bytes of each patch into one patch vector.
Step 3: the latent Transformer, nearly all of the parameters, runs once per patch with a causal mask over patches. This is where the compute savings come from.
Step 4: the local decoder lets byte states query the patch outputs through cross-attention, then predicts each next byte with a 256-way softmax.

blocks.md: **Hash n-gram embeddings.** One byte carries little meaning, so the encoder also looks at the byte n-grams ending at each position, for $n$ from 3 to 8. Storing an embedding for every possible n-gram is impossible, so each n-gram is hashed into a fixed-size table $E_n^{hash}$, one table per $n$, and the looked-up vectors are added to the byte embedding $x_i$. Different n-grams can collide in a slot; the tables are large enough that this is tolerable.

blocks.caption: g_{i,n} = the n bytes ending at position i; a = a 10-digit prime. The sum is normalized by the number of n-gram sizes plus one before entering the encoder.

blocks.title: Hashing the n-grams that end at the t of cat
blocks.code:
a = 1000000007          # a 10-digit prime
E = 500000              # slots per n-gram table
s = b"the cat sat"
i = 6                   # byte t of cat (0-based)
for n in range(3, 9):
    if i + 1 < n:       # not enough history
        continue
    gram = s[i - n + 1 : i + 1]
    h = sum(s[i - j + 1] * a ** (j - 1)
            for j in range(1, n + 1))
    slot = h % E        # row of table E_n

scenes.caption: Position 6 of the cat sat is the t of cat. n = 3 gives the 3-gram cat; its polynomial hash mod 500,000 lands in slot 5646 of table E_3.
n = 4 includes the space before: _cat (space shown as _) hashes to slot 16622 of E_4, a separate table.
n = 5, 6, 7 add more history: e_cat to 259123, he_cat to 7051, the_cat to 154335. Each lookup adds a vector to the byte embedding.

n = 8 needs 8 bytes but only 7 exist up to position 6, so it is skipped (the paper omits n-grams longer than the history). The released code instead zero-pads, offsets byte ids by 4 and gives the oldest byte weight a^0, so its slots differ.

blocks.md: The paper uses 500,000 hash slots per table with n-gram sizes 3 to 8. In a 1B-parameter ablation the hash embeddings gave large gains in bits per byte, the per-n-gram table size mattered most, and smaller n-grams helped more than larger ones. At 8B, going from 500K to 300K slots changed bits per byte by only 0.001.

**Pooling bytes into patches.** The encoder uses cross-attention in the style of the Perceiver: each patch is a query, initialized by max-pooling the byte states in that patch, and the keys and values are byte states. A mask lets each patch attend **only to its own bytes**. Patch vectors are wider than byte vectors, so the attention is split into $k$ heads of byte width that are concatenated into the global width.

blocks.title: Encoder cross-attention mask: which bytes each patch can see

scenes.caption: Using the threshold 1.2 patches of the cat sat: 3 patches over 11 bytes. A 1 means the patch query may attend to that byte. The mask is block-diagonal.
The cat_ patch attends only to bytes 4 to 7. Its query starts as the max-pool of those 4 byte states, and attention then refines it.
The last patch has 3 bytes. Patches vary in length, which is why the authors used PyTorch FlexAttention for these patch-dependent masks.

blocks.md: The **local decoder** reverses the roles: byte states (starting from the encoder's final byte states) are the queries, and the latent Transformer's patch outputs are the keys and values. Cross-attention comes before each decoder layer, and the last layer feeds a 256-way softmax. For the 8B model the paper lists: encoder 1 layer at width 1280 (20M parameters), latent 32 layers at width 4096 (6.4B), decoder 6 layers at width 1280 (120M).

With hash n-gram embeddings, a 1-layer encoder was enough: in the 1B ablation, 1 encoder plus 9 decoder layers reached 0.822 bits per byte versus 0.844 for 5 plus 5. Spend local layers on the decoder, which must produce every byte.

Encoder: bytes plus hashed n-grams, pooled into patch vectors by masked cross-attention. Latent Transformer: the expensive part, once per patch. Decoder: bytes query patch outputs to predict the next byte.

blocks.question: The n-gram 'cat' and some unrelated 3-gram hash to the same slot of $E_3^{hash}$. What happens?
options: Training fails with a key error
They share one embedding vector; the byte embedding and other n-gram sizes still distinguish them
The model falls back to a BPE tokenizer for that word
BLT rehashes until the slot is free
blocks.explain: Hash embeddings accept collisions: both n-grams add the same learned vector. Each position also gets its own byte embedding and five other n-gram lookups, and later layers see the context, so collisions only cost a little. Bigger tables reduce them.

blocks.question: Which part of BLT should get most of the parameters, and why?
options: The latent Transformer, because it runs once per patch, so its cost per byte is divided by the patch size
The local encoder, because it sees every byte
The local decoder, because it has the softmax
The entropy model, because it decides compute
blocks.explain: Cost per byte is about 2(m_g/P + m_l). Parameters in the latent model are amortized over P bytes; parameters in local models are paid on every byte. That is why the 8B model has 6.4B latent and only 140M local parameters.

lessons.title: Results, tradeoffs and where byte models fit

blocks.md: Byte and token models cannot be compared by perplexity, since perplexity is per token. BLT reports **bits per byte**: total cross-entropy loss divided by $\ln 2$ and the number of bytes. It then compares models at equal training FLOPs.

In compute-optimal runs from 1B to 8B parameters on the Llama 2 data, the authors report that entropy-patched BLT matches or beats BPE models trained with the Llama 3 tokenizer. Models with average patches of 6 and 8 bytes land between Llama 2 and Llama 3 tokenizer models while running the big model far less often. The patch-8 model started noticeably worse at 1B but ended better than the Llama 2 tokenizer baseline at 7B.

blocks.title: 8B models at equal training FLOPs (BLT-1T data)

scenes.caption: Average over 7 tasks (ARC-E, ARC-C, HellaSwag, PIQA, MMLU, MBPP, HumanEval). Entropy-patched BLT scores 61.1 versus 60.0 for the BPE model.
Bytes per patch (or per token) on the training mix. Space patching averages 6.1 bytes, so it uses fewer global steps, and pays about 2 points of average score.

blocks.md: The more interesting result is at **fixed inference cost**. For a token model, the inference budget fixes the model size. For BLT, a longer patch frees compute to grow the latent model. Starting from Llama 2 tokenizer models of 470M and 3.6B, the authors built inference-FLOP-matched models: entropy patch size 6 allows a 1.2x to 1.3x larger model, and patch size 8 a 1.6x to 1.7x larger one.

blocks.title: Model size at equal inference FLOPs per byte

scenes.caption: Smaller budget class: 470M, 450M, 610M and 760M non-embedding parameters all cost the same per byte at inference.
Larger class: 3.6B, 3.9B, 5.2B, 6.6B (shown in millions). BPE models win at small training budgets, then BLT overtakes them; the crossover was at about 2.5x to 3x the compute-optimal data.

blocks.md: Reading bytes also changes what the model knows. On noised HellaSwag (random case, dropped or repeated characters, all caps, spaced-out letters) BLT averaged 64.3 versus 56.9 for the BPE model trained on the same 1T tokens. On CUTE, a benchmark of spelling and character manipulation, BLT scored 54.1 versus 27.5, including 99.9 on spelling. It also beat the BPE model on low-resource translation (FLORES-101) by 2 BLEU into English.

scenes.caption: Clean HellaSwag: 79.1, 80.7 and 80.6. On clean text BLT matches the BPE models.
Noised HellaSwag average: 56.9, 64.3, 64.3. Noise hurts everyone, but BLT trained on 1T tokens matches Llama 3.1 trained on far more data.
CUTE (character manipulation): 27.5, 20.0, 54.1. More data did not help Llama 3.1 here; seeing the bytes did.

blocks.md: Limitations the authors list: their FLOP matching is theoretical and the implementation may not yet match token models in wall-clock time; the entropy model is trained separately rather than end to end; and they borrowed BPE scaling-law data ratios that may not be optimal for BLT. BPE still won word deletion and word insertion on CUTE.

You do not have to train from scratch. BLT can be initialized from a token model: the authors copied Llama 3.1's non-embedding weights into the latent Transformer and trained it at one tenth the learning rate of the local models. At the same training FLOPs this raised MMLU from 25.2 (BLT from scratch) to 63.7, against 66.3 for the original Llama 3.1.

Patching is not the only route. **MambaByte** (Wang et al., 2024) keeps every byte but uses a Mamba state-space model, whose memory is a fixed-size state rather than a growing attention cache. To speed up generation it drafts with a subword model and verifies with the byte model, reporting a 2.6x speedup over plain MambaByte decoding.

Byte models trade a tokenizer for an extra design choice: how to group bytes. With learned, entropy-based patches, BLT matched BPE models at 8B for equal training FLOPs, improved robustness and spelling, and turned patch size into a knob that trades steps for model size.

blocks.question: You serve a model under a fixed inference FLOP budget per byte. Why can BLT use a bigger model than a BPE model in the same budget?
options: Byte embeddings are smaller than token embeddings
The entropy model replaces some latent layers
Bigger average patches mean fewer latent steps per byte, so each step can afford more parameters
BLT skips the softmax at inference
blocks.explain: Cost per byte is about 2(m_g/P + m_l). Raising P from about 3.7 (Llama 2 tokens) to 8 lowers the m_g/P term, so m_g can grow while cost per byte stays fixed: 760M versus 470M in the paper's small class. BPE can only lengthen tokens by growing the vocabulary.

blocks.question: A product mainly processes noisy user text (typos, odd casing) in many languages, and needs character-level edits. Which statement best matches the evidence in this course?
options: A BPE model with more training data will close the gap on character tasks
Byte-level models with patching are a strong fit; they were more robust to noise and far better at character manipulation
Byte models only help for English
Byte models are always faster at inference than BPE models
blocks.explain: BLT beat a same-data BPE model by 7.4 points on noised HellaSwag and by 26.6 on CUTE, while Llama 3.1, trained on far more data, scored lower on CUTE. Speed depends on patch size and implementation; the authors note wall-clock parity is not yet shown.
